blocks.text: The chapter’s central claim is that Jesus’ ministry is superior because he is called the mediator of a better covenant, established on better promises. To make that case, Hebrews quotes Jeremiah’s promise of a new covenant in full, including its promises of inwardly written law, shared knowledge of God, and mercy for sins.

The contrast between the earthly sanctuary and the “true tabernacle” is rhetorical and typological: the author uses the earthly pattern to describe a greater heavenly reality. The passage should not be read as if it supplied a complete architectural map of a heavenly sanctuary.

Hebrews quotes Jeremiah from within Jewish Scripture. Later uses of Jeremiah include several kinds of interpretation and reception, so this quotation should not simply be treated as a direct prediction detached from its earlier scriptural setting. Christian fulfillment claims likewise should not erase Israel or turn the covenant contrast into contempt for Judaism, Torah, or living Jewish communities.

The term translated “covenant” may also carry testament-like associations, especially in Hebrews 9:15–17. Here, the immediate argument and the wording of the Greek Jewish Scriptures are important for deciding how the term functions.

The present-tense language about priests offering gifts in verses 4–5 does not by itself establish when Hebrews was written or where its audience lived. Proposed dates on either side of 70 CE and destinations such as Rome or Jerusalem remain disputed.

Hebrews’ use of sanctuary and sacrifice belongs to a later scriptural argument. Reading Leviticus through Hebrews is therefore a later canonical reception and should be distinguished from Leviticus’s own instructions to Israel; Hebrews’ argument also should not make Israelite sanctuary worship meaningless or justify contempt for Jewish worship.

For readers interested in the text’s transmission, Papyrus 46 is an early substantial witness to Hebrews, though it has gaps and its date is approximate. Codex Sinaiticus also preserves Hebrews within its New Testament sequence, after 2 Thessalonians.

sections.title: Reading Hebrews in Its Wider Scriptural Setting
